entries.title: In Tigray, Ethiopian government forces have advanced against a northern rebel group, reports indicate
entries.summary: Reports indicate Ethiopian government forces have made advances against a northern rebel group. Renewed fighting has raised fears the conflict could spill over into the wider region.
entries.content:
Ethiopia

Ethiopia government forces reclaim Tigray capital airport

October 4, 2026

Reports indicate Ethiopian government forces have made advances against a northern rebel group. Renewed fighting has raised fears the conflict could spill over into the wider region.

Government forces in Ethiopia said they have recaptured an airport in Tigray's capital that was seized by rebel groups last week, in the northern region's worst outbreak of violence since a bloody civil war ended in 2022.

Several news agencies cited anonymous government sources on Saturday as saying Ethiopian federal forces now control Alula Aba Nega Airport in Mekelle.

"The military is in full control of the airport. That much I can confirm," an Ethiopian general told the Associated Press on condition of anonymity.

The AFP news agency, citing a "humanitarian source," reported rebel groups were leaving the city as Ethiopian government forces moved in.

Neither side has issued an official statement on the status of who controls Mekelle, and reporting is complicated by communication blackouts and restricted media access.

Return to civil war?

Pulling out of Tigray's capital would be a setback for the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), which recently aligned with several other armed opposition groups in northern Ethiopia.

The TPLF has been the dominant force in Tigray since ousting a government-appointed administration earlier this year, and then appointing former wartime regional leader Debretsion Gebremichael as regional president.

The Addis Ababa-based government's Ethiopian National Defense Force has been fighting off a renewed rebel offensive since late September.

The TPLF seized the airport in Mekelle on September 23, along with launching attacks on government positions in the neighboring regions of Afar and Amhara, initially having made gains before being pushed back this week.

Gebremichael issued a statement on Thursday, promising to continue guerrilla attacks on government forces, similar to what took place when rebels lost control of Mekelle in 2020.

The TPLF, which ruled Ethiopia from 1991 to 2018, seeks to topple Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government. More than 600,000 people were killed in a civil war from 2020 to 2022.

Fears of wider regional unrest

The renewed unrest in northern Ethiopia has led to tensions spilling across the region, with fears of wider regional conflict in the Horn of Africa.

For years, Ethiopia has accused its northern neighbor Eritrea of providing support to Tigray rebels, alongside Sudan and Egypt. All three countries deny this.

Last week, Ethiopia and Eritrea cut diplomatic ties, with both countries expelling diplomats and closing embassies.

The African Union said it was concerned by the growing tensions between Ethiopia, Eritrea and Egypt, and has called on all sides to show maximum restraint.

Eritrea accuses landlocked Ethiopia of planning to invade and seize access to the Red Sea

The TPLF's Debretsion said in his video message that "the war is regional and it is a war to control the Red Sea."

entries.title: Peru: Fire burning on road to Machu Picchu kills 1
entries.summary: One person has died and two others have suffered burns in a fire near the main access route to the historic sanctuary of Machu Picchu.
entries.content:
October 4, 2026

One person has died and two others have suffered burns in a fire near the main access route to the historic sanctuary of Machu Picchu.

A blaze was burning near the main access road to the ancient Inca citadel of Machu Picchu in Peru, leaving one person dead and two injured, officials said on Saturday.

The fire began on Friday in the Sacred Valley of the Cusco region, which also includes the Ollantaytambo train station — the busiest for travelers visiting Machu Picchu.

"We have one elderly person who died in the flames and two others with second-degree burns," Miguel Osco, head of the Cusco Regional Office for Disaster Management and Safety, told RPP radio.

How did the fire start?

Osco said the fire originated from controlled bush burning that farmers carry out to clear land for crops.

The flames spread quickly because of the hot, windy weather and dry vegetation, he added.

The Incas built Machu Picchu in the 15th century.

Located at an altitude of 2,500 meters in the Andes Mountains, the historic sanctuary is regarded as an architectural masterpiece.

UNESCO designated it a World Heritage Site in 1983.

Machu Picchu is Peru's most famous tourist destination, attracting about three million visitors every year.

entries.title: Brazil's 2026 presidential election is kicking off with polls showing Lula and Bolsonaro nearly tied.
entries.summary: Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of former far-right populist President Jair Bolsonaro, is taking on incumbent left-wing President Lula da Silva. Polls show the first round of voting will likely lead to a runoff.
entries.content:
Brazil

Brazil election: Polls show Lula and Bolsonaro neck and neck

October 4, 2026

Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of former far-right populist President Jair Bolsonaro, is taking on incumbent left-wing President Lula da Silva. Polls show the first round of voting will likely lead to a runoff.

The latest polling points to a tight race in Brazil's presidential election on Sunday, with leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva seeking a fourth non-consecutive term and Senator Flavio Bolsonaro seeking to continue the right-wing populist movement started by his father, Jair Bolsonaro.

The two leading candidates wrapped up their campaigns on Saturday in Brazil's economic powerhouse state of Sao Paulo.

Lula vows to 'defeat the far-right'

The 80-year-old Lula capped off his campaign with a tour through the city of Sao Paulo, vowing to "defeat the far right," and framing the election as choice between "democracy and sovereignty" and "barbarism and corruption." Organizers said some 150,000 of Lula's supporters turned up for the rally in Brazil's largest city.

Lula has campaigned on continuing his left-leaning Workers' Party platform, comprising welfare programs, state-funded development and income redistribution.

Bolsonaro's law and order

Flavio Bolsonaro, 45, has served as the Liberal Party's senator for Rio de Janeiro since 2019. On Saturday, he led a motorcycle parade through Sao Paulo's countryside cities of Santa Barbara d'Oeste and Americana.

The right-wing Bolsonaro has campaigned on hardline security policies and tax cuts, emphasizing high cost of living under Lula, who he has slammed as "incompetent."

"I am convinced ​that everything is in place for us to win this election in the first round," the ​lawmaker said.

He also held up a portrait of his father, while the crowd shouted "mito" — a Portuguese word for "legend" that Jair Bolsonaro's supporters use to refer to him.

Brazil's 2022 election rematch

The elder Bolsonaro is currently serving a 27-year sentence in prison for attempting a coup to overturn his loss to Lula in the 2022 presidential election. Flavio Bolsonaro has vowed to pardon his father if elected.

Lula's team has cast the Bolsonaro movement as a threat to Brazil's sovereignty, pointing to Flavio and Jair's ties with US President Donald Trump, who year slapped a 50% tariff on Brazilian imports in response to Jair Bolsonaro's coup trial, which the US president called a "witch hunt."

The younger Bolsonaro has said in interviews he is "more moderate" than his father, who he has nevertheless said will remain "my compass, my point of reference."

Policies where both Bolsonaros are similar include relaxed gun control laws and skepticism of human-caused climate change.

Trump has not endorsed the senator, but has said he is watching the election "very closely."

What happens next?

Brazil finds itself politically divided, and campaigning has been bitter, with online operations from both sides seizing on every gaffe, accusation and rumor, quickly producing slick videos or AI-generated images for social media.

In September, it was revealed Bolsonaro is under investigation for alleged corruption, money laundering and tax evasion tied to the financing of a biopic about his father. He has denied any misconduct. 

Polls show neither candidate is likely to win more than 50% of valid votes on Sunday needed to avoid a runoff that would take place on October 25.

The latest polling for the first round of voting shows Lula at 46% and Bolsonaro at 45%, according to the Brazilian data intelligence and public opinion research firm Quaest cited by Reuters news agency.

In the case of a run-off, the Quaest poll shows Lula at 42% and Bolsonaro at 44%.

In 2022, Lula beat Jair Bolsonaro by only 1.8 percentage points.

Along with voting for president, Brazil's 160 million registered voters are also choosing other lawmakers, governors, and some senators.

entries.title: AI giants 'not being nearly careful enough,' warns outgoing OpenAI safety engineer
entries.summary: Days after President Donald Trump signed a voluntary pact with artificial intelligence giants, a former OpenAI worker said his industry needs the same safeguards as nuclear power or aviation.
entries.content:
October 3, 2026

Days after President Donald Trump signed a voluntary pact with artificial intelligence giants, a former OpenAI worker said his industry needs the same safeguards as nuclear power or aviation.

A safety engineer who recently quit ChatGPTcreator OpenAI warned Saturday that artificial intelligence (AI) firms were "not being nearly careful enough."

David Robinson's comments come amid growing concerns about AI becoming too powerful — a threat that US President Donald Trump has labeled a "hoax."

OpenAI and Anthropic recently disclosed cases in which their AI models slipped past safety controls, hid mistakes and hacked systems they were not meant to access.

What did David Robinson write?

In an op-ed for The Atlantic, Robinson said AI needs guardrails similar to those for nuclear power and aviation, adding, "The time for trial and error is over."

He called for more emphasis on safety and research before US Big Tech develops more advanced AI models "so that the occasional and inevitable human error does not open a door to disaster."

Robinson, who oversaw safety reports for 12 frontier AI-model launches, said the recent errors were typical because tech giants are prioritizing "speed and flexibility."

"An environment where things like this can happen is no place to grow artificial minds that could be smarter than we are and that might not do what we want them to."

The former OpenAI employee noted that the firm relies on "iterative deployment." It releases new AI models first and only tightens safeguards after problems show up.

"As ​the company sprints from one launch to the next, it is failing to achieve the ​level of care ‌that I believe is needed," Robinson, who worked at OpenAI for 3 1/2 years, added.

ChatGPT creator insists AI is safe

OpenAI reacted to the latest criticism in a statement, "We're making sure our models don't become more capable than we can safely manage ​and secure, and ⁠we pause training or hold back models when we need to slow down."

In recent months, there have been repeated warnings from technology experts and policymakers that AI models are advancing so fast they could take control and possibly wipe out humanity.

Despite those fears, US President Donald Trump is vehemently against stronger regulation, insisting that it will slow down innovation and make it harder for US AI models to beat Chinese rivals.

This week, Trump announced a voluntary safety pact with six companies — Nvidia, SpaceX, OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta and Alphabet's Google.

The president described the deal as "morally binding,” even if it is not legally enforceable.

He also directed his administration to rename AI as "Super Intelligence" or SI.

A survey by Reuters/Ipsos last month found that three-quarters of Americans worry that AI giants are not doing enough to stop AI from causing serious harm to society.

entries.title: Pakistan vs. Afghanistan: From allies and neighbors to war
entries.summary: For years, Pakistan supported the Taliban in Afghanistan. But now Pakistan is bombing its neighbor. How the former allies became adversaries and why negotiations keep failing.
entries.content:
Middle East

Pakistan vs. Afghanistan: From allies and neighbors to war

October 3, 2026

For years, Pakistan supported the Taliban in Afghanistan. But now Pakistan is bombing its neighbor. How the former allies became adversaries and why negotiations keep failing.

On Thursday night, Pakistan attacked targets in Afghanistan. The results of that attack are disputed. The Taliban, the Islamic fundamentalist nationalist movement that controls Afghanistan, says that between nine and 10 civilians were killed, including women and children. But Pakistan claims the strike killed 22 militants and destroyed weapons and ammunition depots.

These early October attacks are just the latest escalation in a conflict between the two countries that reignited mid-September, after months of comparative calm.

The conflict was sparked again after a series of attacks on Pakistani security forces. On September 18, an attack on a police compound in the northwestern city of Kohat resulted in the deaths of 31 people and more than 100 injured. A splinter group belonging to the Pakistani Taliban, also known as Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan, or TTP, claimed responsibility for the attack in Kohat, in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, bordering Afghanistan.

Pakistan accused Afghanistan of providing the TTP with a safe haven. Afghanistan denies this but clashes at the border and then airstrikes by Pakistan followed.

TTP and Taliban: A complex relationship

The TTP in Pakistan is not the same as Afghanistan's Taliban. Although it does have close ideological and personnel ties to the Afghan Taliban, it is an independent organization that fights the Pakistani state.

Many of its fighters sided with the Taliban during that country's long-running insurgency against international and US troops. This is why, after the Taliban returned to power in 2021, the TTP gained more room and more leverage. This has meant that Afghanistan — a former ally of Pakistan — has increasingly become a threat to its neighbor.

Pakistan has asked the Taliban to take action against the TTP, but the close connection between the two make this difficult.

"Because of these personal connections and networks, it is extremely difficult for the Afghan Taliban to break away," says Conrad Schetter, director of the Bonn International Center for Conflict Studies, or BICC.

The connections don't mean that the Taliban has any control over the TTP. There are certainly historical connections between the two, but Schetter doesn't believe that equals any sort of strong, direct influence.

"The Taliban are simply not prepared to take orders from Islamabad," adds Thomas Ruttig, co-director of the Afghanistan Analysts Network, a think tank working between Kabul and Berlin. "They won't let anyone outside interfere."

This means the Pakistani policy of supporting the Taliban in order to gain influence in Afghanistan hasn't worked.

Difficult borders

There's also another older conflict that has an impact on the current situation. This involves what is known as the Durand Line, drawn in 1893 by a British diplomat and an Afghan emir to mark spheres of influence between British India and Afghanistan.

The current border between Afghanistan and Pakistan follows the Durand Line and also divides an area on both sides, homeland to Pashtuns, who make up the largest ethnic group in Afghanistan and second largest in Pakistan.

So the border dispute here isn't just about territory, it's also about identity.

"Ethnic and nationalist elements play a significant role in the conflict," Schetter tells DW. Many Pashtuns still refuse to accept the border that the Durand Line created.

In Pakistan, the country's long-running rivalry with India also plays a part. A friendly Afghanistan would have been advantageous for Pakistan. But India has also strengthened its ties to the Taliban.

"While Islamabad once viewed Afghanistan as a source of 'strategic depth' in its rivalry with India, it now increasingly views its north-western neighbor as a liability," an analysis by British think tank Chatham House notes.

Pakistan exerts pressure

Pakistan still has power over Afghanistan, though. As a landlocked country, Afghanistan relies on trade routes through neighboring countries, and Pakistan in particular. Pakistan can use border closures and trade restrictions to exert pressure even as the Taliban regime is trying to reduce dependence on Pakistan and find new economic and political partners.

Trade and security considerations are now becoming tangled. Pakistan has held talks with the TTP that were mediated by the Taliban and ceasefires were agreed upon. Talks between Pakistan and Afghanistan also took place. But none of the temporary agreements resolved the crucial question of how to prevent attacks on Pakistan from Afghan territory.

So in parallel with diplomacy, Pakistan has also been relying on economic and political pressure, for example, by closing borders and restricting trade and by sending Afghan refugees back into Afghanistan.

An analysis by the US-based Council on Foreign Relations notes that the Taliban are worried that if they crack down on the TTP too hard, they will drive the group towards another extremist militant group, the Islamic State in Khorasan Province or IS-K. This group opposes the Taliban.

The conflict recently escalated to another level. At the end of September, Kabul reported 28 killed and 32 captured fighters who had infiltrated Afghanistan from Nuristan province, Pakistan. The Taliban accused Pakistan of supporting its armed opponents, something Pakistan has denied.

"It is known from past decades that Pakistan has regularly supported armed groups on the Afghan side — for example, the Mujahideen during the Soviet occupation and later the Taliban," Ruttig points out. "What's new though is that Pakistan apparently also supports parts of today's armed anti-Taliban opposition."

Significant escalation

This is turning the dispute over the TTP into a larger conflict in which both sides accuse each other of supporting armed groups from the other's territory.

British think tank Chatham House speaks of a significant escalation compared to previous border skirmishes. Worryingly, a conflict over armed groups and border incidents is turning into a direct confrontation between the two nation states.

Ruttig believes that it would be possible to contain the spiraling violence if both sides return to negotiations.

"If both sides were willing to return to the negotiating table — perhaps with international mediation —there would be ways to contain the conflict and, above all, to protect the civilian population on both sides," he argues.

In a late September commentary in Pakistani weekly magazine The Friday Times, Pakistani analyst Saqib Ali Khan advocates for several things that could ease the tensions. That includes a reliable channel between Islamabad and Kabul, a separate approach for armed groups and greater involvement of the population along the border.

The conflict, he argues, is not merely a dispute between two governments but also a security, border, economic and regional conflict.

"Along those lines, there would have to be a shift in perspective on both sides," Schetter concludes.

In the long term, greater economic integration is also needed, he adds, so that Pakistan and Afghanistan do not define their relationship solely through security and power issues.

This story was originally published in German.

entries.title: Tennessee's prison chief resigns after botched execution of murderer Christa Pike
entries.summary: Prison commissioner Frank Strada insisted his team followed protocol, even after two doses of anesthetic failed to kill convicted murderer Christa Pike. He is set to leave his post this month.
entries.content:
October 3, 2026

Prison commissioner Frank Strada insisted his team followed protocol, even after two doses of anesthetic failed to kill convicted murderer Christa Pike. He is set to leave his post this month.

The head of the prison system in the US state of Tennessee is resigning after the execution of convicted murderer Christa Pike went wrong, the state governor said Saturday.

Witnesses said Pike was still breathing and moaning after two doses of the anesthetic pentobarbital failed to kill her during Wednesday's procedure.

The attempt was halted and she was transferred to hospital in critical condition.

It was the second time this year that an execution in the southern state had to be halted.

What do we know about the resignation?

Governor Bill Lee said in a statement that prison commissioner Frank Strada would leave his post sometime this month.

Lee said he thanked Strada for "his willingness to put the interests of Tennesseans first during this difficult moment."

In the same statement, Strada acknowledged that: "Stepping aside is in the best interest of Tennesseans as the independent review moves forward."

He said the department had carried out its responsibilities in accordance with established protocol, but called the review "entirely appropriate and necessary."

The state has halted further executions until the review has been completed.

Strada took on the role in January 2023. Nearly two years later, he announced that Tennessee would, from then on, only use pentobarbital for lethal injections of death-row inmates.

What went wrong?

Tennessee authorities have yet to explain why Pike survived.

Her attorneys said they believed problems with the IV lines caused the pentobarbital to flow into her body instead of her bloodstream.

Pike's lawyers said Friday that she is unconsciousand on a ventilator in hospital.

While they welcomed Strada's departure, her legal team said, “It does nothing to help Christa now.”

"What happened to her Wednesday reflects a systemic failure that goes far beyond any one person," the four-lawyer team said.

"We hope the governor's call for a full, independent review will expose the profound problems within Tennessee’s entire death penalty system," it added.

Had the drugs killed Pike, she would have been the first woman executed by the state since 1820.

Pike was sentenced to death in 1996, aged 20, for the murder of Colleen Slemmer, whom Pike was convinced was trying to steal her boyfriend.

Slemmer, who was 19, was tortured and killed in a remote area near the University of Tennessee in Knoxville.

Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko

entries.title: Latvia: Ruling party leads in exit polls amid populist gains
entries.summary: According to an exit poll by public broadcaster LSM, Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs' centerist party, United List, was projected to win 35.6% of the vote.
entries.content:
Latvia

Latvia: Ruling party leads in exit polls amid populist gains

Published October 3, 2026last updated October 3, 2026

According to an exit poll by public broadcaster LSM, Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs' centerist party, United List, was projected to win 35.6% of the vote.

The party of Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs took a comfortable lead in parliamentary elections on Saturday, exit polls showed.

Kulbergs' centerist, pro-Ukraine party, United List, was projected to win 35.6% of the vote, according to an exit poll by public proadcaster LSM.

"It's remarkably ‌good. ​I was not expecting such result," Kulbergs said at his party's headquarters in Riga.

The exit poll put the the populist Latvia First party in second place with 11.3% — nearly double its share at the last election in 2022. It had courted the country's substantial ethnic Russian minority.

Kulbergs said on Saturday night that he would not cooperate with any pro-Russian parties and specifically ruled out forming a coaltition with Latvia First.

Some 1.5 million people were eligible to vote in the country's 11th parliamentary election since independence from the Soviet Union in 1991.

The election, which saw 100 seats in the Saeima being contested by 14 parties using a proportional system, has been dominated by rising living costs and national security concerns in the small Baltic country which borders both Russia and Belarus.

Kulbergs, has only been in office since May after the previous government collapsed over a dispute about Ukrainian drones. Despite his party leading opinion polls, his coalition is expected to emerge weakened as populist parties gain.

Latvia vote shaped by Russia concerns

Russia's ongoing invasion of Ukraine is seen as a direct threat to national security in Latvia which, like Ukraine, is a former Soviet state with a sizeable ethnic Russian and Russian-speaking minority.

Unlike Ukraine, however, Latvia is a member of both the European Union and NATO.

Riga is one of Kyiv's closest partners and supporters, having committed itself by law to spending at least 5% of GDP on defense – leaving less room for spending elsewhere.

Many Latvians complain of high prices and low wages, the economy is sluggish, the health system is under strain, and emigration and an ageing population remain persistent challenges.

Populist movements such as the Sovereign Power/Young Latvians Alliance and the Latvia First party have attempted to exploit discontent by taking a less stringent line towards Moscow and arguing that a complete economic decoupling from Russia is damaging.

German Eurofighter jets in Latvian airspace

Nevertheless, no parties are proposing any major deviation from Latvia's clear foreign policy alignment with the EU and NATO.

Indeed, four German Eurofighter jets have been deployed to protect Latvian airspace during the election in response to a request from Riga.

Once ballots are counted, attention is likely to shift quickly to coalition negotiations, which could prove lengthy and complex.

Partial results are expected on Saturday evening, with preliminary official results due on Sunday.

Edited by: Natalie Muller

entries.title: Ukraine to step up oil attacks as Russia hits Kyiv bridges
entries.summary: As Moscow intensifies attacks on Kyiv and other cities, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has vowed to hit Russian energy infrastructure.
entries.content:
Published October 3, 2026last updated October 3, 2026

As Moscow intensifies attacks on Kyiv and other cities, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has vowed to hit Russian energy infrastructure.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Saturday vowed to continue hitting Russia's oil refineries in retaliation for what he called Moscow's new strategy of targeting major Ukrainian cities for intensive air strikes.

Ukraine has accused the Kremlin of stepping up attacks on civilian targets in recent days, to force residents to leave urban areas of the country before winter.

In strikes over the past two days, Russian forces have also hit two major bridges crossing the Dnipro River in the capital, Kyiv.

What did Zelenskyy say?

In an interview with Reuters news agency, Zelenskyy said Ukrainian intelligence agencies had uncovered details of a "new doctrine" from Russian President Vladimir Putin.

"We saw documents and we know that they allow them to attack infrastructure ... logistics ... roads, schools, hospitals, to pressure people to leave the capital, leave different cities," Zelenskyy warned.

The Ukrainian leader said that Kyiv would "respond in any way (we can) ... First of all, oil refiners: who give money to them [Russia] for this war. But we will not respond, of course, like them, on any ‌civilian objects."

Second Kyiv bridge struck

This week marks the first time Moscow has targeted the bridges across the Dnipro River connecting east and west Kyiv.

Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said Saturday that the Northern Bridge over the river was struck by Russian forces from the air.

In a statement posted on Telegram, Klitschko said two people were injured and the road surface and trolleybus wires on the bridge were damaged.

"Traffic across the bridge from the left bank to the right bank is currently blocked," he said.

Over the past two days, Kyiv's Southern Bridge has been hit several times by a volley of strikes by Russian drones.

The attacks caused traffic chaos, with long lines of stationary cars and buses clogging major roads.

A total of eight bridges connect Kyiv's western and eastern banks along the Dnipro River.

Russia urges foreign diplomats, nationals to leave Kyiv

Russia's Foreign Ministry on Saturday, meanwhile, warned foreign diplomats and nationals in Kyiv to leave the city, adding that "individuals are knowingly exposing themselves to mortal danger."

"The Armed Forces of the Russian Federation will continue to deliver massive retaliatory strikes," it said, while adding that "responsibility for any potential negative consequences rests entirely with those who ignore this warning."

In the years following its February 2022 invasion of Ukraine, Russia has frequently targeted Kyiv with overnight drone attacks.

Moscow has previously denied a systematic targeting of civilians during its bombings.

Moldova denounces latest Russian strike on Ukraine

Moldovan President Maia Sandu condemned the latest Russian attack on Kyiv and complained about a violation of her country's airspace.

"Its war is dangerously reaching Moldova," Sandu said in a post on X. "5 Russian air attack weapons, including Banderol missiles and drones, violated our airspace and exploded on our soil."

"Moscow is putting lives at risk across Europe and must be stopped," Sandu said.

The Moldovan Foreign Ministry summoned the Russian ambassador and urged Moscow to prevent such incidents.

Moldova is a strong supporter of Ukraine, and its airspace is frequently violated due to Russian attacks on its neighbor.

Russian forces are stationed in the Moldovan breakaway province of Transnistria, raising fears that Moldova could be the next target of invasion after Ukraine.    

Edited by: Natalie Muller, Dmytro Hubenko

entries.title: UK remands 2 Iranians over alleged antisemitic terror plot
entries.summary: The pair were arrested on the eve of Yom Kippur and later charged with plotting to attack Jewish targets in Manchester.
entries.content:
October 3, 2026

The pair were arrested on the eve of Yom Kippur and later charged with plotting to attack Jewish targets in Manchester.

Two Iranian nationals charged with plotting acts of terrorism  against the United Kingdom's Jewish community were remanded in custody by a court in London on Saturday.

The pair were detained on September 20, the eve of Yom Kippur, the holiest day in the Jewish calendar.

The case only came to light on Friday when the two men were charged, just days after another terror plot, which the UK has linked to Iran, was foiled.

What do we know about the case?

Prosecutor Mark Luckett told Westminster Magistrates' Court that Rahman S., 34, and Salam ‌A., 36, are accused of carrying out "hostile reconnaissance" on Jewish targets in Manchester, northern England.

He said the two men planned to use a "homemade explosive device" and had allegedly been in contact with a third party, an Iranian national, most likely operating from within Iran.

The contact is alleged to have given the pair instructions on how ‌to put together a homemade device from chlorine and brake fluid, the court heard.

Luckett said the two suspects had used online resources, including images, plans and maps, to identify and research potential attack sites.

He told the court that the targets included the Manchester Jewish Museum and the Heaton Park synagogue, where two Jewish worshippers were killed in a knife attack a year ago on Friday.

The two Iranian suspects had arrived in Britain in small boats that crossed the English Channel from mainland Europe, Luckett added.

One had been granted asylum, while the other's application is still pending, the court heard.

The pair did not enter a plea and were remanded in custody until their next hearing at London's Old Bailey on October 23.

Vicki Evans, senior national coordinator of counterterror policing, said the plot was believed to be isolated and there was no ongoing public threat.

Police find no link to RAF Fairford plot

Evans also said the Manchester plot was "not connected in any way" to the suspected terror plot at RAF Fairford last weekend, which Prime Minister Andy Burnham said showed "strong indications" of Iranian involvement.

Also on Saturday, police said a dual British-Iranian national, arrested on Thursday in connection with the RAF Fairford plot, was released on police bail.

The 25-year-old was the sixth person arrested and then bailed as the investigation continues.

Police said the five other men held are all British nationals in their 20s and from London.

Police uncovered the RAF Fairford plot when a farmer spotted suspicious white vans near the base early on Sunday morning and called the authorities. Officers found petrol inside the vans, but no explosives.

UK media reported this week that one of the suspects dialled the police about an hour earlier, though that has not been confirmed.

Tehran has rejected as baseless accusations of targeting RAF Fairford, which lies 90 miles (145 kilometers) west of London and has been used by US bombers to strike Iran.

The UK remains on high alert for potential threats from Russia and Iran.

Iran has previously used proxies to commit crimes on British soil, including repeated attacks and plots against Jewish targets, as well as against dissidents.

Antisemitic attacks more broadly have risen sharply since Hamas attacked Israel on 7 October 2023.

Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko

entries.title: Spain: Massive protests after housing bills voted down
entries.summary: Organizers estimated that 500,000 people turned out in the streets of Madrid to demand affordable housing. Similar protests were held in around 50 other Spanish cities.
entries.content:
Spain

Spain: Massive protests after housing bills voted down

October 3, 2026

Organizers estimated that 500,000 people turned out in the streets of Madrid to demand affordable housing. Similar protests were held in around 50 other Spanish cities.

Tens of thousands of people protested across Spain on Saturday to demand affordable housing.

The protests come a day after the Spanish parliament narrowly voted down two emergency bills designed to support renters and prevent evictions.

"It only proves that it is us the people who have to adapt ‌to the political parties, and not the politicians to ‌what ​the people want, and this can't go on like that," one 26-year-old protester in Madrid told the Reuters news agency.

They are the latest demonstrations in a week-long wave of actions that began in response to the eviction of an 87-year-old woman, Maricarmen Abascalin, in Madrid.

"What we are feeling in the streets is a new energy that we haven't seen in a long time, and energy that is showing that eight days of people's power can achieve more than eight years of progressive government," said Valeria Racu, one of the spokespeople of the Tenants' Union organizing Saturday's protest.

Protests in dozens of cities

Police said around 70,000 people took part in the demonstration in Madrid. Organizers put the figure closer to 500,000 people.

Additional protests were held in around 50 other cities.

In the eastern city of Valencia, police used tear gas and rubber bullets against protesters.

Dozens of protesters had managed to get inside Valencia's City of Arts and Sciences — a major landmark in the city — before they were ejected by police.

What's next for the Spanish government?

Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez's proposed emergency measures included automatic renewal of tenancy contracts and restrictions on evicting vulnerable tenants. However, bills were shot down by opposition parties on Friday.

This defeat infuriated those who had been protesting against the country's increasingly unaffordable housing market all week.

"We are demanding a fundamental right: decent housing, stability and conditions allowing us to construct a decent life project," another protester in Madrid, aged 31, told the AFP news agency.

Spanish media reported that Sanchez might call a snap election for November after the legislation failed to pass, adding that the government would be watching Saturday's protests closely before making a decision.

Sanchez's office declined to comment on the reports.
